name: Surrealism
info: Surrealism is an art and cultural movement that developed in Europe after the First World War, in which artists and writers sought to let the unconscious mind express itself, and which Breton's manifesto of 1924 gave an official start.

facts.where: Paris was the most important centre; autonomous groups in Brussels and London, a second English group in Birmingham, Chile, Japan and Martinique; from the 1930s the idea spread to North America, South America, Central America, the Caribbean and Asia, and in the 1940s New York became a place of exile
facts.period: the word coined by Guillaume Apollinaire in 1917; Dada years after the First World War; manifestos of October 1924; expansion in the mid-1920s; the 1930s described as a golden age; exile and the Second World War; Breton's return to France after the war; death of Breton in 1966; groups still active today
facts.figures: André Breton, leader of the Paris group and author of the manifestos; Louis Aragon, Paul Éluard and Benjamin Péret, writers; Max Ernst, Joan Miró, André Masson and Yves Tanguy, painters; Salvador Dalí and René Magritte, who created the most widely recognised images of the movement; Man Ray, photographer; Luis Buñuel, film-maker; Yvan Goll, leader of a rival faction
facts.outcome: Breton's group won the right to the name in 1924 but the movement was marked by fractures, resignations and expulsions; its ideas passed into Abstract Expressionism, the Beat writers, the Theatre of the Absurd and the events of May 1968, and Surrealist groups continue to publish and exhibit

t: Surrealism aimed, in Breton's words, to resolve the previously contradictory conditions of dream and reality into an absolute reality, a super-reality, and Breton held it to be above all a revolutionary movement.
Two rival groups published manifestos in October 1924, Yvan Goll's on 1 October and Breton's on 15 October, and Breton's group won the right to the term.

The movement was repeatedly divided over politics and membership, yet it spread to many countries and influenced Abstract Expressionism, the Beat writers, the Theatre of the Absurd and the French revolt of May 1968.
dyk: In 1938 the Paris Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme was lit only by a single light bulb over a coal brazier, with 1,200 coal bags hung from the ceiling, and visitors were given flashlights to view the art.
ev: Guillaume Apollinaire uses the word surrealism in his notes for the ballet Parade, which premiers on 18 May
Breton and Soupault publish The Magnetic Fields, written with automatic techniques
Yvan Goll publishes his Manifeste du surréalisme on 1 October and Breton publishes his on 15 October
La Peinture Surrealiste, the first Surrealist exhibition, is held at Galerie Pierre in Paris
The second Surrealist manifesto excludes members unwilling to commit to collective action, and the excluded respond with the pamphlet Un Cadavre
The London International Surrealist Exhibition is organised by Herbert Read, with an introduction by Breton
The Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme opens at the Beaux-arts Gallery in Paris, and the Chilean group La Mandrágora is founded
André Breton dies, and Surrealist groups continue without him

sections.background:
The word surrealism was first coined in March 1917 by Guillaume Apollinaire. In a letter to Paul Dermée he wrote that, all things considered, it was better to adopt surrealism than supernaturalism, which he had first used. He then described Parade, the Ballets Russes work that premiered on 18 May 1917, as a kind of surrealism. Jean Cocteau wrote its one-act scenario and Erik Satie its music. Apollinaire also took the term up again as the subtitle of his play Les Mamelles de Tirésias, which was written in 1903 and first performed in 1917.

The First World War scattered the writers and artists who had been based in Paris, and many became involved with Dada, believing that excessive rational thought and bourgeois values had brought the conflict upon the world. During the war André Breton, who had trained in medicine and psychiatry, served in a neurological hospital where he used Sigmund Freud's psychoanalytic methods with soldiers suffering from shell-shock. There he met the young writer Jacques Vaché, whose anti-social attitude and disdain for established artistic tradition he admired.

Back in Paris, Breton joined in Dada activities and started the literary journal Littérature with Louis Aragon and Philippe Soupault. They experimented with automatic writing, writing spontaneously without censoring their thoughts, and published the results and accounts of dreams in the magazine. Breton and Soupault published The Magnetic Fields in 1920.
sections.aims:
Breton defined Surrealism in his 1924 manifesto as pure psychic automatism, by which one proposes to express, verbally, in writing or in any other manner, the real functioning of thought, in the absence of all control exercised by reason and outside all aesthetic and moral preoccupation. Its encyclopedic definition rested on a belief in the superior reality of certain neglected forms of association, in the omnipotence of dream and in the disinterested play of thought. Freud's free association and dream analysis were of crucial importance to the Surrealists, who embraced idiosyncrasy while rejecting the idea of an underlying madness. Dalí later proclaimed, "There is only one difference between a madman and me. I am not mad."

The Surrealists also stressed that elements not normally found together could be combined in one frame to produce illogical and startling effects. Breton took this idea of startling juxtapositions from a 1918 essay by the poet Pierre Reverdy, who held that the more distant and true the relationship between two juxtaposed realities, the stronger the image.

The group aimed to revolutionise human experience in its personal, cultural, social and political aspects, and to free people from false rationality and restrictive customs and structures. Breton proclaimed that the true aim of Surrealism was "long live the social revolution, and it alone!" At various times Surrealists aligned with communism and anarchism, and they looked to the Hegelian and Marxist dialectic.
sections.events:
By October 1924 two rival groups had formed. One, led by Yvan Goll, included Tristan Tzara, Francis Picabia and Pierre Reverdy; the other was led by Breton. Goll published his Manifeste du surréalisme on 1 October 1924 and Breton published his, through Éditions du Sagittaire, on 15 October. The two men clashed openly at the Comédie des Champs-Élysées, at one point literally fighting, and Breton won through tactical and numerical superiority. That year the Bureau of Surrealist Research was established and began publishing La Révolution surréaliste. In 1925 an autonomous group formed in Brussels, and the first Surrealist exhibition, La Peinture Surrealiste, was held at Galerie Pierre in Paris.

In 1929 Breton asked Surrealists to assess their degree of moral competence, and the second manifesto excluded anyone reluctant to commit to collective action. The excluded members attacked Breton in the pamphlet Un Cadavre. In 1933 the Surrealists' assertion that a proletarian literature within a capitalist society was impossible led to their break with the Association des Ecrivains et Artistes Révolutionnaires and the expulsion of Breton, Éluard and Crevel from the Communist Party.

The 1936 London International Surrealist Exhibition and the 1938 Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme in Paris followed. During the Second World War many artists fled to North America, and Breton went to the United States in 1941. After the war the Paris group, led by Breton, decided to embrace anarchism explicitly.
sections.people:
André Breton led the Paris group and wrote its manifestos. His group came to include Paul Éluard, Benjamin Péret, René Crevel, Robert Desnos, Max Ernst, Salvador Dalí, Luis Buñuel, Man Ray, Hans Arp, Joan Miró, Yves Tanguy, Dora Maar and others. Breton admired Pablo Picasso and Marcel Duchamp and courted them to join, but they remained peripheral. Aragon and Philippe Soupault were with him from the days of Littérature, though Aragon left the group after committing himself to the French Communist Party in 1932.

Painters and sculptors joined as the mid-1920s went on, among them Giorgio de Chirico, Alberto Giacometti, Valentine Hugo, Méret Oppenheim, Toyen and Kansuke Yamamoto. André Masson's automatic drawings of 1923 are often used as the point at which the visual arts were accepted and the break from Dada made. The Brussels group included E. L. T. Mesens, René Magritte, Paul Nougé, Marcel Lecomte and André Souris. Dalí joined the group in 1929, and he and Magritte created the most widely recognised images of the movement.

Others were expelled or left. Antonin Artaud and Roger Vitrac, who co-founded the Theatre Alfred Jarry, were expelled, and Dalí was considered by Breton and his associates to have betrayed and left Surrealism. Peggy Guggenheim married Max Ernst and promoted the work of other Surrealists. Breton declared Frida Kahlo an innate Surrealist painter after meeting her in Mexico in 1938.
sections.outcomes:
Breton's victory over Goll in 1924 did not end the quarrels. From that moment the history of Surrealism remained marked by fractures, resignations and resounding excommunications, each Surrealist having a personal view of the issue and goals and accepting more or less the definitions laid out by Breton. Breton's group refused to put the proletarian struggle before radical creation, which made the late 1920s a turbulent time for the group and the Communist Party alike, and many people close to Breton, notably Aragon, left to work with the Communists.

The disunion of 1929 and 1930 had very little negative effect on Surrealism as Breton saw it, since Aragon, Crevel, Dalí and Buñuel remained true to group action for the time being. The success, or controversy, of Dalí and Buñuel's film L'Age d'Or in December 1930 drew new recruits. Breton himself later admitted that the centrality of automatic writing had been overstated, and collage and other methods were introduced.

In New York, artists such as Arshile Gorky, Jackson Pollock and Robert Motherwell converged closely with the exiled Surrealists, albeit with some suspicion and reservations. Abstract Expressionism grew directly out of the meeting of New York artists with European Surrealists, and until the emergence of Pop art Surrealism can be seen as the single most important influence on the sudden growth of American arts.
sections.legacy:
Breton died in 1966. Jean Schuster disbanded the original Paris Surrealist Group in 1969, but another Parisian group was formed later. The Group of Czech-Slovak Surrealists never disbanded and continues to publish its journal Analogon, and groups in Chicago, Leeds and Stockholm have also continued. Jan Švankmajer of the Czech-Slovak group continues to make films and experiment with objects.

The Surrealist idea reached well beyond the arts. Anticolonial writers of the Négritude movement in Martinique took up Surrealism as a revolutionary method, and their journal Tropiques was first published in 1941. In the 1960s the Situationist International was closely associated with Surrealism, and among the slogans painted on the walls of the Sorbonne in May 1968 were familiar Surrealist ones. In Poland the Orange Alternative, created in 1981 by Waldemar Fydrych, used Surrealist symbolism in its happenings during the Jaruzelski regime.

Writers of the Beat Generation, among them Philip Lamantia and Ted Joans, were influenced by Surrealism, and Allen Ginsberg cited Artaud as a direct influence on Howl. The critic Martin Esslin argued that the playwrights he grouped as the Theatre of the Absurd could trace similarities to the Surrealists. Surrealist art remains popular with museum visitors: in 2001 an exhibition at Tate Modern attracted over 170,000 visitors, and Surrealism Beyond Borders in 2021 and 2022 brought together work from 45 or more countries.

summary: Surrealism was an art and cultural movement that developed in Europe after the First World War, with Paris as its most important centre. Its members sought to let the unconscious express itself, and Breton held it to be above all a revolutionary movement. Its groups quarrelled and divided, but it spread across the world and its groups still exist.
references: David Hopkins, Dada and Surrealism: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford University Press, 2004)
notes: start 1924: the article says the movement was not officially established until after October 1924, though the word dates from 1917 and Breton's group was working with automatic writing from 1919-1920. Nothing in the article gives an end; groups continue today, so end is null.
The article says the 1924 manifestos were published two weeks apart (Goll 1 October, Breton 15 October); the lede says Goll published two weeks prior. Consistent.
The article describes the Brussels group as formed in 1925 and says Goemans and Magritte moved to Paris in 1927, but Goemans is not named in the group list; I left Goemans out.
The article lists both the 'Surrealist Manifesto' dates and a 1925 Declaration of 27 January; left out for length, as were the Abd-el-Krim letter and the 1932 'Murderous Humanitarianism' text.

The 1938 Paris exhibition and the founding of La Mandrágora in 1938 share one event entry; the entry is the 1938 exhibition and the Chilean group is a second item in the same sentence. Editor may split them.
The section on Surrealist films lists Destino (2003) and other films; films, songs and similar works about the movement were left out under the job rules, as were the music and photography sections.
Dalí's support for capitalism and for Franco is in the article; I said only that Breton's circle considered him to have betrayed and left Surrealism.
The article gives 1966 as Breton's death only in the Surrealist groups section; the 1969 disbanding is by Jean Schuster.
The Dalí exclusion is dated by the article only as 'excommunicated'; no year given, so none stated. The article also says Artaud and Vitrac were expelled (Vitrac in 1926; Artaud no year).

The Beat and May 1968 passages: the article's slogan 'All power to the imagination' attribution is garbled (quoted by Situationists and Enragés from the Marxist 'Rêvé-lutionary' theory of Breton's group); left out.
